newsitem.title: UK: Rise in aircraft building propels titanium demand.
newsitem.headline: Rise in aircraft building propels titanium demand.

text.p: A takeoff in aircraft orders backed by help from the humble golf club have rejeuvenated titanium's fortunes, propelling producers towards much needed profits after a string of losses.

"Boeing and Airbus keep reporting higher build rates and increasing backlog, and that should bode well for titanium for years to come," said Dennis Kelly, chief financial officer of U.S. producer Oregon Metallurgical Corp .
John Monahan, vice president sales and marketing for Tremont Corp's Timet added, "We just reflect what's going on in Boeing and golf, and 1997 will definitely be strong."
Next week the light metal's newly-found luster competes with the bright lights of Las Vegas where delegates gather for the International Titanium Association's meeting.
"There are certainly a lot of expectations built into the share price," said analyst Victor Lazarovici of Smith Barney in New York. "Growth continues for the foreseeable future."
Western production is dominated by the big three U.S. West Coast producers, Timet, RMI Titanium Corp, and Oregon Metallurgical.
The turnaround in titanium's fortunes has seen RMI's share price rise from just $2 in July 1994 to $24 by Thursday's close. Oregon's share price has tripled to $33 since last Fall.
"We expect the market next year to be up 10 percent in volume," said John Odle, RMI's executive vice president.
Brokerages such as Merrill Lynch, Smith Barney and Salomon Brothers have shown more interest in titanium equities.
Merrill Lynch expected supply/demand to tighten over the next two to three years. "The titanium industry is beginning a cycle that may see several years of increased demand," the broker said.

Timet's Monahan forecast world wide titanium production of 100 million lbs (about 45,000 tonnes) in 1996, rising to 110 million pounds next year. Production capacity is about 120 million pounds. Over half of demand is in the United States.
Shipments recently peaked at 225 million pounds in 1989 and reached a nadir of 91 million in 1994 after military aircraft spending collapsed.

Anti-corrosion applications such as tube and strip in power plants and chemical processes represent half of demand, with a further 40 percent used in defense and civil aircraft making. Golf clubs account for the balance.

Kelly said titanium consumption in golf drivers has soared from 1.5 million pounds two years ago to nine million this year. "Certainly we think it will continue to grow as they look to go from drivers to other fairway woods and probably into the irons," he added.

But within five to eight years the golf industry will look for a different "wonder metal" to use, Kelly said. But golf clubs helped demystify titanium's exotic image and make it more open to other new applications, he added.
"Golf clubs are a new market but in comparison to aerospace, it's of no consequence," said Jim Hannah of U.K.'s Willan-Wogen titanium processor. "People are blowing that out of proportion."
Nevertheless, the titanium industry is developing new uses even if the golf market ends in the rough.

Timet is working with the car industry in Detroit to use titanium in suspension springs and exhaust systems, while RMI is researching into oil and gas pipe applications. Oregon is pushing ahead with using titanium plate to protect the Swedish-built Leopard tank, replacing heavier steel.

The U.S. and Russia are the world's largest producers and Smith Barney's Lazarovici said titanium prices were rising because there was no spare production capacity in the west, and Former Soviet Union capacity was underused.
